title: Launch Brief (Draft) — Quantization Profile Library (Opt-in, Route-level)
content:
Owner: Marissa Cole (Product — Optimize)
Last edited: 2025-03-11
Status: DRAFT (for internal alignment)


1) Summary / What we’re launching
We’re launching an opt-in Quantization Profile Library that publishes per-model quantization profiles and allows customers to enable a profile at the route level (and optionally by region/deployment tier, depending on their setup).

This is a serving feature focused on improving unit economics (cost/token) while preserving quality and staying within latency SLOs.

Key principles:
- Opt-in only for v1. Default behavior unchanged if you do nothing.
- Route-level controls (not global tenant defaults) to keep blast radius small.
- Deterministic selection + guardrails: if incompatible, we fall back to baseline precision.
- Auditable + reversible changes (Console + APIs + audit log events).

What this is NOT (v1):
- No auto-recommendations per customer.
- No auto-tuning in production.
- Not default-on across all models/routes.


2) Target audience
Primary personas:
- ML Engineers / Applied ML teams: want lower inference cost but need guardrails + eval guidance.
- Platform/Infra engineers: need predictable routing behavior, deterministic configs, rollback, and audit logs.
- Engineering leads / cost owners: want measurable savings and clarity on operational risk.

Secondary:
- SRE / on-call operators: need dashboards, fast rollback, kill switch, and crisp runbooks.
- Security/compliance (enterprise): want RBAC, auditability, change control story.

Customer segments:
- AI-native startups with scaling token spend and willingness to trial opt-in optimizations.
- Mid-market / enterprise teams using Dedicated and/or Private where costs are meaningful and changes must be controlled.


3) Positioning
Positioning statement:
Quantization Profile Library is a safe, opt-in way to reduce inference cost per token by applying Redwood-validated quantization profiles per model, enabled at the route level with deterministic selection, compatibility checks, and easy rollback.

How we should talk about it (internal + external):
- “Library of validated profiles” rather than “magic optimization.”
- Emphasize controls + safety: compatibility checks, fallbacks, audit logs.
- Encourage proper evaluation and staged rollout: A/B test on a route, monitor quality/latency, then expand.

Suggested short blurb:
“Enable Redwood-validated quantization profiles per route to reduce costs while preserving quality—fully opt-in with compatibility guardrails, observability, and one-click rollback.”

Differentiators to highlight:
- Route-level blast radius control.
- Deterministic profile resolution (no surprises).
- Publishing cadence + versioning (profiles evolve; customers can pin).
- Observability signals: applied vs fallback, fallback rate, latency deltas.


4) Scope (Beta vs GA)
Beta scope (target: 2–3 design partners):
- Hosted + Dedicated coverage (Private: case-by-case if ready).
- Console toggle + Config API support for selecting a profile for a route.
- Compatibility warnings surfaced in Console/API; safe fallback to baseline.
- Baseline vs quantized comparison guidance + playbook for route-level evals.
- Dashboards: enabled state, fallback rate, p95 latency, error rate, cost/token deltas where available.
- Global kill switch (SRE-only) with audit trail.

GA scope (guided by PM-642):
- Broader model coverage in the library, plus clearer docs on compatibility matrix.
- More polished Console UX (change history/changelog, previews).
- Support playbook and escalation routing.

Non-goals (keep repeating):
- Auto-enable for existing routes.
- “Recommended/latest” aliases that can silently change behavior without customer action (if we add aliases later, we need explicit semantics and communication).


5) Launch strategy / rollout plan
Phases:
A) Internal readiness
- Confirm schema stability + profile lifecycle (author → validate → publish → deprecate).
- Confirm control plane determinism + caching behavior under load.
- Confirm runtime observability tags (quant_profile_id, applied/fallback/disabled).
- Confirm rollback procedure + kill switch exercise (game day recommended).

B) Beta (design partner only)
- Customers explicitly opt into beta + get allowlisted if needed.
- Start with 1 route, 1 region, small traffic percentage.
- Run route-level A/B evals and monitor for a defined soak period.
- Expand route-by-route after passing thresholds.

C) GA
- Public docs + release notes.
- Self-serve enablement in Console/API where allowed.
- Continued publishing cadence with clear labeling (stable vs experimental).

Gating criteria (high level):
- No statistically significant quality regression beyond agreed thresholds on Redwood prompt sets + design partner evals.
- Stable p95 latency within agreed band.
- Fallback behavior works (and does not loop) under incompatibility.
- Clear operational story: dashboards, alerts, rollback.


6) Messaging pillars + proof points
Pillar 1: Cost reduction with guardrails
- Proof: benchmark deltas (where publishable) and design partner results.
- Claim discipline: avoid promising universal savings; frame as “typical savings on supported models/workloads.”

Pillar 2: Control and predictability
- Route-level opt-in; canary + rollback.
- Deterministic resolution; pinned profile versions.

Pillar 3: Operational readiness
- Observability: applied vs fallback; per-route visibility.
- Audit log events for change control; RBAC.


7) Beta plan (design partners)
Targets: 2–3 design partners (see PM-643).
Candidate profiles:
- Start with a small set of high-volume models with strong benchmark signal and known-safe constraints.

Beta success criteria (per partner):
- Demonstrated reduction in cost/token on at least one high-volume route.
- No material quality regression in partner’s representative prompt sets.
- No sustained p95 latency regression beyond agreed band.
- Partner can self-serve: enable/disable, interpret dashboards, and understand fallback behavior.

Partner commitments (set expectations upfront):
- They will run evals (we provide playbook + harness support as needed).
- They will stage rollout (small traffic, soak, expand).
- They will notify us before enabling across multiple routes/regions.

Redwood commitments:
- On-call coverage during enablement windows (for beta).
- Clear rollback SLA and kill switch availability.
- Weekly check-in cadence (30 min) during initial rollout.


8) Release notes outline (public)
Title:
Quantization Profile Library (Opt-in): route-level quantization profiles with compatibility guardrails

Body (suggested bullets):
- New: Opt-in Quantization Profile Library for supported models.
- Control: Enable quantization per route (and optionally by region/tier) via Console and API.
- Safety: Compatibility checks with automatic fallback to baseline precision.
- Observability: Metrics and logs indicating whether a profile was applied or fell back.
- Operations: Audit log trail for enable/disable and profile changes; emergency kill switch (platform-managed).

What customers should do:
- Pick a low-risk route.
- Run a baseline vs quantized evaluation.
- Enable with canary traffic; monitor dashboards; expand gradually.

Docs links (to include):
- How to enable per route
- Compatibility limitations
- Troubleshooting and rollback


9) Comms plan checklist
Internal comms
- #eng-ml: publish profile authoring + validation workflow summary and publishing cadence.
- #eng-runtime / #eng-platform: confirm final behavior of fallback, determinism, caching.
- #eng-sre / on-call: share runbooks, dashboard links, alert thresholds, kill switch procedure.
- Support (CS + Support): share troubleshooting guide + escalation paths.

External comms (Beta)
- Direct outreach to design partners with enablement steps + eval playbook + monitoring checklist.
- Schedule enablement window and success metrics review.

External comms (GA)
- Release notes entry.
- Docs announcement/update.
- Optional blog post or short “what’s new” (TBD; keep claims conservative).


10) Sales/CS enablement notes
What to say:
- “This is opt-in per route. You can test on a low-risk route first.”
- “If the profile is incompatible for your model/hardware/constraints, Redwood will fall back safely.”
- “You’ll be able to see applied vs fallback in metrics/logs.”

What NOT to say:
- “It will always be cheaper” or “no quality impact guaranteed.”
- “Recommended profiles will update automatically” (we are not doing silent changes).

Assets needed:
- 1-pager (internal) with:
  - Supported models list (or how to find it)
  - Expected savings ranges (where we have confidence)
  - Quick risk assessment + rollback instructions
- Security FAQ:
  - Audit logs fields
  - RBAC roles
  - Change history retention


11) FAQ (draft)
Q: Can I enable this across my whole account?
A: v1 is route-level opt-in. This is intentional to keep blast radius small.

Q: What happens if I enable a profile that doesn’t work for my hardware?
A: The platform evaluates compatibility and will block with an actionable error where possible. If a mismatch is encountered at runtime/policy evaluation, it falls back to baseline precision.

Q: How do I know whether quantization was actually applied?
A: Use metrics/log annotations (quant_profile_id and resolution outcome applied/fallback/disabled) and the rollout dashboard panels.

Q: How do I roll back?
A: Disable the profile at the route level. In an emergency, SRE can flip the global kill switch. Confirm recovery via fallback rate + latency/error dashboards.

Q: Does this change my prompts or outputs?
A: Quantization can change outputs. We recommend running route-level A/B evals using representative prompt sets and monitoring quality metrics.


12) Risks and mitigations (what we should be honest about)
Risk: Quality regressions on specific tasks/prompt sets.
- Mitigation: offline eval gates, regression thresholds, staged rollout, rapid disable.

Risk: Latency regressions due to kernel path or caching interactions.
- Mitigation: perf suite coverage, perf-canary comparisons, dashboards + alerts.

Risk: Operational load (registry metadata thundering herd).
- Mitigation: caching, rate limiting, and safe fallbacks already in plan.

Risk: Customer confusion about “profile versioning” vs “model versioning.”
- Mitigation: docs and Console copy must clearly distinguish model version pinning and profile version pinning.


13) Open questions / TODOs
- Final decision on how we present profile identifiers in Console: explicit pinned version only vs optional alias.
- Public compatibility matrix format (docs vs Console-driven lookup).
- Whether GA is allowlisted by default for first N weeks.
- Confirm exact audit log export fields needed for enterprise (route identifiers, actor, before/after, profile id).


Appendix: Draft timeline (placeholder)
- Week 0: finalize docs + dashboards + runbooks; finish internal game day
- Week 1: Beta partner 1 enablement (1 route, 1 region, 1% traffic)
- Week 2–3: expand to partner 2–3; incorporate feedback; publish additional profiles
- GA target: after passing gating criteria + support readiness

(End of doc)
